newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn eager to defuse gold dispute with Bundesbank.
newsitem.headline: Bonn eager to defuse gold dispute with Bundesbank.

text.p: The German government was searching for a face-saving compromise with the Bundesbank on Friday after the central bank firmly rejected Bonn's plan to revalue assets to retire old debt and qualify for Europe's single currency.

Leaders from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) stressed the Bundesbank supported the basic plan to revalue the reserves towards market rates and opposed only the timing.

Clearly eager to defuse the dispute with one of the world's most trusted and powerful central banks, Bonn officials nevertheless pointed out there was nothing the Bundesbank could do to prevent legislation to revalue the reserves this year.

"We should refrain from using the word 'conflict'," government spokesman Peter Hausmann said. "There is no dispute about the need to revalue the reserves or about their use. The only discussion we are having is about the timing."

The remarkably public dispute between the government and the Bundesbank erupted when the Frankfurt-based central bank criticised Bonn's plans to revalue its gold and currency assets. But the government said it would go ahead regardless.

"The revaluation is a political decision and advice from the Bundesbank cannot replace the legislature's competence," said Peter Hintze, general secretary of the CDU. Hintze also rejected calls for Finance Minister Theo Waigel to resign.

Waigel wants to revalue the bank's reserves to give a much-needed injection of cash to Bonn's public finances as it scrambles to cut back its deficits to make the grade for European monetary union (EMU).

But the Bundesbank warned that Bonn's scheme -- which calls for a special profit transfer to be made this year and next on the basis of the higher valuation of gold and currency reserves -- could undermine the euro from the start.

The central bank condemned the plan as "interference" in its monetary policy and said it was not in line with changes which must be made to central bank balance sheets ahead of the transfer of monetary policy power to a European central bank.

"The only thing in dispute is whether (the revaluation) will happen in this year or not until 1999," said Hermann Otto Solms, the FDP leader in parliament. "But to put it bluntly, what is correct for 1999 can't be completely wrong in 1998 or 1997."

Solms said in an interview with SWF radio that the government could have better prepared the ground for the revaluation and said the timing should have been better. But he said both sides agreed that the reserves needed to be revalued.
"The reality is that this is a debate about prestige more than facts," Solms said.

EU nations wanting to join the first wave of monetary union must, according to the Maastricht Treaty, have a 1997 budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP.

To overcome the stalemate, which was driving down share prices across Europe and gave the dollar a lift on Friday against the deutschemark, some government and Bundesbank leaders were floating compromise solutions.
Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said that one way out of the dispute would be for the government to drop its demand for a payout of a special profit and leave the matter to the Bundesbank.

Welteke said that even if the Bundesbank did not have any formal instruments to defend itself against the government plans, members of parliament would be wise to note that the public's confidence in the transition to the planned euro stemmed from the Bundesbank, not from politicians.
"They should take care that no political damage is done here," Welteke said.

Peter Mueller, a leading young ally of Kohl and head of the CDU in Saar state, urged the cash-strapped government to calm down and take a relaxed view of the Maastricht Treaty's three percent budget deficit target.

"We have manoeuvered ourselves into a situation the treaty does not require," he said. "A reasonable look at the Maastricht treaty shows there is no obligation to have a deficit of 3.0 percent. There is room to manoeuvre and we should use it."

The first cracks in the Kohl government's 12-seat parliamentary majority emerged on Friday when CDU deputy Juergen Augustinowitz said he would not vote for the legislation against the Bundesbank's will.
"I will not take part in any decision in the German Bundestag (lower house of parliament) which would impair the stability of the mark or the independence and credibility of the Bundesbank," he said.
